transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Redwood SE), Alex Mercer (SableGrid CTO), Priya Narayan (Head of Security), Jonah Lee (Network Engineer), Tara Singh (Compliance)

Auto-generated summary (brief, may be incomplete):
- Deep dive on private deployment network isolation patterns, egress controls, and key management (KMS) integration.
- Customer concerns: audit log retention, data residency for EU customers, RBAC/SSO interplay with local AD, and air-gapped upgrade story.
- Agreed next steps: share SOC2 artifacts, send VPC zoning diagram, scope two-node pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: All right hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood inference, and Diego and Evelyn are with me. Alex, Priya, thanks for making time. Can we do quick intros?
[00:00:12] Alex: Yeah Alex Mercer, CTO at SableGrid Energy. We're building edge control plane for microgrids and we need the inference stack to live inside our colo for regulatory reasons.
[00:00:21] Priya: Priya, head of security, I'll be driving the compliance checklist.
[00:00:24] Jonah: Jonah, network eng, i'll be implementing the firewalls and routing.
[00:00:27] Maya: Great. Goal for today is to walk through our private deploy model and map to your network and compliance asks: SOC 2/ISO mapping, RBAC/SSO, audit logs, KMS, egress patterns. We'll pause for questions.
[00:00:40] Diego: Quick note — when we say private deploy, there are two flavors: VPC-backed private with a Redwood-managed control plane, and fully on-prem where control plane is customer-hosted. We should clarify which you want.
[00:00:50] Alex: For SableGrid we need customer control plane in our VPC and the inference nodes inside our on-prem colo racks. No public egress for inferencing tokens unless explicitly allowed.
[00:00:59] Evelyn: Ok got it. That suggests a hardened control plane endpoint inside your mgmt subnet and tightly scoped cross-subnet rules.
[00:01:06] Priya: A few compliance items up front: SOC 2 evidence for access reviews, ISO 27001 mapping, audit log retention minimum 1 year for core logs and 7 years for some operational event types. Also EU data residency partitioning for a set of customers.
[00:01:21] Maya: We will share our SOC 2 Type II summary and a sanitized audit log sample. For residency — we support region pinning of logs and can configure log sinks to customer Splunk or S3 with SSE-KMS.
[00:01:31] Jonah: How does KMS work for the private control plane? Do you have to bring your own key or can you integrate with our HSM?
[00:01:36] Diego: We support BYOK via standard KMS integrations. For on-prem HSMs we provide an offline keywrap flow — basically the service can be configured to use your key material; we do not export plaintext keys. There have been some customers using Luna/Thales.
[00:01:49] Jonah: Ok, good.
[00:01:51] Tara: A process question — if we rotate keys, what's the impact on running KV cache/state on inferencing nodes?
[00:01:55] Diego: Rotations are targeted: we use envelope encryption. KV cache at runtime is cached in memory; persisted artifacts (model checkpoints, any cached blobs written to disk) are encrypted with the KMS envelope key. Rotation triggers re-wrap of persisted blobs and rolling restart policy for nodes that need to re-sync. The runtime keeps local ephemeral keys so that short lived in-memory state doesn't get stalled during rotation.
[00:02:18] Alex: So we won't have to stop inference during rotation?
[00:02:20] Diego: Correct — we can do rolling rewraps and keep traffic on the nodes not yet rotated, typical pattern. We'll send a writeup on rotation steps.
[00:02:28] [00:02:30] Maya: Can we jump into network zoning? Jonah, do you want to sketch the zones you have today?
[00:02:35] Jonah: Sure. At the colo we have mgmt VLANs for orchestration, a compute VLAN for workloads, and an edge VLAN for customer endpoints. Egress to the internet is via an egress proxy cluster — we enforce outbound ACLs there.
[00:02:47] Evelyn: Good, that maps well. Our recommendation is 4 logical zones: management (control plane), inference compute, storage/backup, and a bastion/ops zone. All control-plane traffic should be restricted to mgmt subnet and use mutual TLS.
[00:03:00] Priya: How does SSO/RBAC tie into the control plane? We run Okta + AD.
[00:03:05] Diego: We support SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is role-based at the token and route level: you can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (admin, ops, read-only). For on-prem we can federate against your AD via LDAP or AD FS.
[00:03:20] Alex: Are audit logs immutable? We want tamper-evident logs.
[00:03:24] Maya: We ship logs to your chosen sink; for immutability we recommend writing logs to an append-only S3 bucket with object lock or to a tamper-evident SIEM. We also support signing of log batches. We'll include a doc showing examples.
[00:03:36] Jonah: For egress — we cannot have direct internet egress from compute VLAN. Can Redwood's runtime proxy to our egress cluster?
[00:03:42] Diego: Yes, the runtime can be configured to route all external model fetch/checkpoint calls through your egress proxy via NAT gateway or an internal egress appliance. There is an option for strict deny with allowlist for specific endpoints (model store, licensing).
[00:03:56] Jonah: What's the connectivity expectation for telemetry? We need to know if metrics/traces leave the colo.
[00:04:01] Evelyn: Telemetry can be scraped locally and shipped to your observability stack (Prometheus pushgateway or remote write). We don't require outbound metrics to Redwood unless you opt into managed telemetry support.
[00:04:12] Priya: Any third-party agents on nodes? I.e., do you require DaemonSets that could be flagged by our SCAP scans?
[00:04:18] Diego: We have a small runtime agent for KV cache and process supervision. For on-prem installs we provide an auditable manifest, and the agent runs as an unprivileged process. We can provide SBOMs and signed binaries.
[00:04:29] Alex: Patch and upgrade story — can we stage patches in an airgapped manner? We have to push signed images via internal registry.
[00:04:35] Evelyn: Yes — for airgapped installs we support an offline install bundle and signed image tarballs. The control plane has an import routine that validates signatures against the customer's trust root.
[00:04:45] Maya: Let's talk about firewall policies in practice. Diego, can you outline recommended ACLs between zones?
[00:04:50] Diego: Sure. High-level: control-plane -> inference compute: mutual TLS on port 443 for control plane APIs; SSH locked to bastion only (or use SSM-like gateway); Storage access via internal service account with ephemeral credentials. Ingress from edge devices to inference nodes should terminate at a gateway that does request validation — we recommend not opening direct inbound to compute nodes.
[00:05:07] Jonah: So no public ELB direct to nodes, we use an internal API gateway?
[00:05:10] Diego: Correct, internal gateway + WAF if needed. Also recommend egress rules on compute nodes to only allow DNS and proxy outbound to the egress cluster.
[00:05:19] Tara: On audit logs: what are the event types you capture by default?
[00:05:23] Evelyn: Auth events (login, token refresh), admin actions (role changes, deployments), model actions (model pull, model version change), runtime events (node up/down, restart, OOM), and network events (failed mTLS handshake).
[00:05:36] Priya: Can we increase retention per event class? e.g., longer retention for admin actions.
[00:05:40] Maya: Yes, retention slices are configurable; we can map ACLs and retention classes and push to different buckets or SIEM indices.
[00:05:46] [00:05:50] Alex: A tricky one — our customers require regional isolation. We may host EU customer inference on separate racks. Is there any cross-talk risk with your control plane metadata?
[00:05:58] Diego: Metadata is segregated by tenant and region, and you can pin model artifacts to the local model registry in your region. Our control plane will not replicate EU tenants to US regions if you opt-out. We'll document the tenancy isolation guarantees.
[00:06:12] Jonah: Network-level — do you need any inbound VPN or peering to the Redwood maintenance plane?
[00:06:16] Maya: For fully customer-hosted control plane, we don't need inbound peering. Occasionally we offer a maintenance VPN for support sessions but only with explicit ticket-based approval and limited lifetime credentials. Many enterprises prefer no-peering and file support bundles.
[00:06:30] Priya: What about intrusion detection / host-based sensors, do you integrate with our IDS?
[00:06:34] Diego: We can emit logs and network flow metrics to your IDS. For host-based sensors we can expose traces via eBPF or syslog; this is configurable and we avoid bundling anything that conflicts with endpoint security.
[00:06:45] Tara: On SAML sync — will provisioning create service accounts automatically or do we prefer manual onboarding?
[00:06:51] Evelyn: There is an optional SCIM bridge that can provision users and groups. Many customers do group-to-role mapping and then disable manual provisioning for compliance.
[00:06:59] Alex: Let's go through a concrete egress scenario: a model update fetches from Redwood model store. We want that to go through our egress proxy and be logged. How does the runtime authenticate to your model store?
[00:07:10] Diego: Options: 1) Use short-lived signed URLs that your egress logs like any other request; 2) mirror model artifacts into your local model registry and the runtime pulls locally — that's the pattern we might prefer for airgapped. Signed URLs are TLS + signature; we also support mutual TLS client certs.
[00:07:25] Jonah: For mirrored model registry, what's the sync cadence and checksum guarantee?
[00:07:29] Diego: We can provide an rsync-style digest-based sync plus manifest verification. Sync cadence is policy driven — on-demand for releases or periodic for nightly.
[00:07:37] [00:07:38] Maya: Quick question from Tara: do we have examples of audit log formats that meet financial regulator requirements?
[00:07:43] Evelyn: We'll attach sample log schema; they are JSON-lines with event_id, timestamp, actor, action, resource, outcome, and tenant_id. We have a mapping doc for SOC 2 controls.
[00:07:55] Priya: About RBAC — can we implement just-in-time admin elevation for emergency operations?
[00:07:59] Diego: Yes we support a JIT workflow via SAML where a temporary elevated role is granted and that action is audited and can be tied to a ticket ID.
[00:08:07] Jonah: On firewall specifics — do you recommend stateful or stateless for compute egress?
[00:08:11] Diego: Stateful is recommended for short-lived flows; stateful with strict timeouts and connection tracking. For high-throughput inference it's important to ensure conntrack table sizing is adequate. We'll include recommended conntrack params.
[00:08:22] Alex: For compression and token streaming, do we ever require long lived TCP connections that might be killed by proxies?
[00:08:27] Diego: Streaming uses long-lived websockets/HTTP2 sessions; ensure your egress proxy supports long-lived sessions or we can provide a proxy keepalive config.
[00:08:36] [00:08:40] Tara: Who owns PII redaction and model outputs? If model outputs contain customer-sensitive content, what's Redwood's stance?
[00:08:47] Maya: For private deploys, you control the data plane; Redwood does not persist PII outside configured sinks. We can enable PII filters and redact before logs leave the inference nodes. We'll share options.
[00:08:58] Priya: Do you support FIPS-compliant ciphers for TLS?
[00:09:02] Diego: Yes. FIPS-ready builds are available and we can lock cipher suites and crypto modules to FIPS-approved ones in the control plane.
[00:09:10] Alex: Let's surface any residual risks or tradeoffs — Diego?
[00:09:14] Diego: Biggest tradeoffs: full airgap increases operational overhead for updates and telemetry; BYOK/HSM gives more control but complicates disaster recovery; stricter egress deny rules reduce blast radius but require mirrored registries for timely updates. We'll help you quantify.
[00:09:30] Maya: Ok, let's do an ask/response run so we capture answers for your compliance checklist.
[00:09:34] Alex: Q1: Can Redwood provide on-site onboarding and a signed security NDA for engineers?
[00:09:38] Maya: Yes — we have an engineer on-site program and can execute a one-off NDA.
[00:09:42] Jonah: Q2: Does the installer require root privileges?
[00:09:45] Diego: The installation requires admin account but we run components as unprivileged processes; we'll provide an install checklist for ESM.
[00:09:52] Priya: Q3: Do you support SIEM forwarding to our Splunk instance over TLS with client certs?
[00:09:56] Evelyn: Yes — we support forwarding via Syslog over TLS or direct Splunk HEC with token or mutual TLS.
[00:10:04] Tara: Q4: Are your binaries signed and do you provide SBOM?
[00:10:08] Diego: Yes, signed pkcs7 artifacts and full SBOM available on request.
[00:10:12] [00:10:20] Maya: We're at about 10 minutes in — we'll pivot into a short demo of the control plane UI and then back to questions.
[00:10:25] [Demo noise / screen share; transcription lower fidelity]
[00:11:30] Diego: (demo) Here is the project, tenant settings, the key management tab — you can see KMS integration, the mapping of roles to Okta groups, and the audit logs viewer. If we click into a log entry you can see request headers and outcome.
[00:11:50] Alex: The audit viewer — can we export with signatures?
[00:11:53] Diego: You can export batched, and we sign export bundles.
[00:12:05] Priya: Regarding network hardening, can you provide sample IPTables/ACL snippets?
[00:12:10] Evelyn: Yes we'll include sample iptables and Palo Alto rules.
[00:12:16] Jonah: We use Fortinet — do you have vendor-specific examples?
[00:12:19] Diego: We have a firewall rule cookbook that includes Palo Alto, Fortinet, and Cisco ASA examples. We'll attach that.
[00:12:26] Alex: For the pilot, our goals are: validate no-internet egress for inference, test KMS rotation without downtime, and verify audit log immutability. Timeline: pilot in June.
[00:12:36] Maya: Sounds good. We'll scope a 2-week pilot: 2 inference nodes, one control plane vm in your VPC, mirrored model registry, and egress through your proxy.
[00:12:44] Priya: For the immutability test, we'll want to see object lock and signed log bundles.
[00:12:49] Evelyn: We'll demonstrate both patterns in the pilot.
[00:12:52] Jonah: About metrics retention — do you recommend remote write to our long-term Prometheus?
[00:12:56] Diego: Yes remote write to your TSDB is recommended for long-term retention; local Prometheus can be used for short-term alerting.
[00:13:05] [00:13:10] Maya: Quick recaps of blockers: Alex — confirm CIDRs and egress appliance details; Priya — confirm retention windows; Jonah — confirm Fortinet appliance models; Redwood — share SOC2 artifacts, SBOM, firewall cookbook.
[00:13:25] Alex: We'll get those to you by Friday.
[00:13:28] Maya: Great. Any last questions?
[00:13:31] Priya: One last — how is incident response handled for private deploys? Who gets paged?
[00:13:36] Diego: For private deploys we can integrate with your PagerDuty and map incidents to roles. Support escalation flows are defined in the runbook; for topology issues we typically follow customer-first escalation. We'll provide an incident runbook sample.
[00:13:49] Tara: Do you keep a tamper log of support sessions and remote maintenance actions?
[00:13:53] Evelyn: Yes — all support sessions require ticket IDs and limited-time VPN; sessions are recorded in the audit log with signed entries.
[00:14:02] Maya: Ok thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff.
[00:14:07] Alex: Thanks, useful session.
[00:14:09] [Meeting ends - remaining minutes were Q&A and screenshare as noted. Transcription ends; some sections may be imperfectly transcribed.]

References / attachments mentioned (links or short notes):
